segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when he opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven for about half an hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I saw the seven angels who stand before God, and seven trumpets were given to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Another angel came and stood at the altar, holding a golden censer, and he was given much incense to offer with the prayers of all the holy ones on the golden altar that is before the throne.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the holy ones, rose from the angel’s hand before God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the angel took the censer and filled it with fire from the altar and threw it to the earth, and there came thunder and rumblings and flashes of lightning and an earthquake.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to blow them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The first blew his trumpet, and there came hail and fire mixed with blood, and it was thrown to the earth. A third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all the green grass was burned up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The second angel blew his trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea. A third of the sea became blood,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: a third of the creatures in the sea—those that had life—died, and a third of the ships were destroyed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The third angel blew his trumpet, and a great star fell from the sky, blazing like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of water.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The name of the star is Wormwood. A third of the waters turned to wormwood, and many people died from the waters, because they had been made bitter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The fourth angel blew his trumpet, and a third of the sun was struck, and a third of the moon, and a third of the stars, so that a third of them would be darkened, and the day would not shine for a third of it, and the night likewise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then I looked, and I heard an eagle flying in midheaven, saying in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Woe, woe, woe to those who live on the earth, because of the remaining trumpet blasts of the three angels who are about to blow!”

notes.note: The meaning of the silence is not explained and is disputed. Some connect it with the hush of awe before God’s judgment found in the prophets; others think heaven falls silent so that the prayers of verses 3–4 can be heard. Either way, it is a dramatic pause before the trumpets.

notes.phrase: the seven angels who stand before God
notes.note: The definite article suggests a group the readers already knew. Jewish tradition spoke of seven chief angels who stand in God’s presence (compare Tobit 12:15), and most interpreters think these are meant.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep, while others use “God’s people.” “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue, whereas the Greek word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel.

The Greek has a bare dative, “to give to/for the prayers.” Most translations take it as “with the prayers,” the incense accompanying them as they rise. It can also be read as “on behalf of the prayers,” or as identifying the incense with the prayers, as in 5:8. The same construction recurs in verse 4.

notes.phrase: A third of the earth was burned up
notes.note: This clause is absent from the late manuscripts behind the King James Version, which therefore lacks it. The earliest and best manuscripts include it, and it was probably dropped by a copyist whose eye skipped between the three repeated endings “was burned up.”

The same Greek word covers both God’s dwelling and the visible sky. Older translations have “from heaven” here. A falling star belongs to the visible sky, so “sky” is used, while verse 1 keeps “heaven” for the scene at God’s throne.

Wormwood is an intensely bitter plant. In the Hebrew Scriptures, wormwood and bitter or poisoned water are images of God’s judgment and of the bitterness of suffering (for example Jeremiah 9:15). The plant itself is not normally deadly, so the star’s name evokes that imagery of judgment and is not a botanical description.

The late manuscripts behind the King James Version read “angel” here. The earliest and best manuscripts read “eagle,” and modern editions and translations follow them. The change to “angel” is probably a copyist’s attempt to supply a more expected speaker.

The Greek word is an astronomical term for the zenith, the highest point of the sky where the sun stands at noon. The eagle flies where everyone on earth can see and hear it. Some translations render it “directly overhead” or “high in the air.”

candidates.reason: The word shifts between “earth,” “land” and “ground” across the New Testament, and in Revelation the choice affects how global the judgments sound.

candidates.rendering: those who live on the earth
candidates.reason: The phrase οἱ κατοικοῦντες ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς is a recurring technical expression in Revelation for humanity opposed to God and should be rendered identically each time.
It occurs three times in Revelation (8:13; 14:6; 19:17), and translations vary between “midheaven,” “directly overhead” and “midair.”
It recurs across the Gospels and Revelation; translators differ between “woe to,” “how terrible for” and “alas,” and Revelation’s numbered “woes” depend on a fixed rendering.
It recurs through the trumpet series and elsewhere (Matt 6:2; 1 Cor 15:52); “blow” and “sound” are both common, and the series needs a uniform rendering.
